title: DOW-UAP-D56, Range Fouler Debrief, Arabian Sea, August 2020
what_is_it: A standardized U.S. Navy Range Fouler Debrief Form used to report an unauthorized intrusion of unidentified objects into controlled airspace during military operations.
core_summary: On August 24, 2020, a U.S. Navy pilot from HSM-73 observed three unidentified small air contacts while conducting routine operations over the North Arabian Sea at night. The pilot initially tracked one contact before losing sight of it behind a cloud, then upon regaining contact observed two additional objects to the east. All three contacts appeared to maintain their relative course, speed, and altitude, with no interaction between the aircraft and the unknown contacts.
redaction_evidence: moderate — reporter's name, email address, and certain contact information are redacted under (b)(6) exemption; some form fields are partially obscured but the narrative and key data fields are largely intact
interpretation_warnings: Single-source report based entirely on one pilot's subjective observations during a nighttime encounter.
No corroborating sensor data (radar, IFF, or electronic support) was obtained — all tracking was apparently visual only.
Distance to the contacts was unknown, making size, speed, and altitude estimates unreliable.
The contacts' speed and precise course were unknown to the observer; the westerly heading was described as an appearance rather than a measured value.
The description 'wings/airframe' and 'round' may reflect the observer's best interpretation under nighttime conditions with unknown distance.
Reporter's identifying information is redacted under (b)(6), preventing independent verification of the account.
The form notes that 'all descriptive and estimative language reflects the reporter's subjective interpretation at the time of the event.'

public_headline: Navy Pilot Reported Three Unidentified Objects Over Arabian Sea in 2020
public_tldr: A U.S. Navy debrief form documents a nighttime encounter on August 24, 2020, in which a pilot from helicopter squadron HSM-73 visually observed three unidentified airborne objects over the North Arabian Sea. No radar, transponder, or electronic sensor data corroborated the sighting, and the distance, speed, and precise course of the objects were all unknown to the observer.
public_narrative:
This document is a U.S. Navy "Range Fouler" debrief form — a standardized report used when unidentified objects intrude into controlled military airspace. It was filed by a pilot (rank O-3, roughly Lieutenant Commander level) assigned to HSM-73, a Navy helicopter squadron, following an incident during routine operations over the North Arabian Sea on the night of August 24, 2020.

According to the report, the pilot first spotted a single unknown airborne contact at approximately 00:04 Zulu time. After tracking it visually, the pilot lost sight of the object when it passed behind a cloud. Upon reacquiring the first contact, the pilot noticed two additional objects to the east of the original one — bringing the total to three. All three appeared to hold a steady course, speed, and altitude, heading roughly westward. The pilot described the objects as having a wings-or-airframe structure and a round shape.

Critically, no instrument data backed up the visual observation. The report states there was no stable radar track, no electronic support measures, and no IFF (Identification Friend or Foe) transponder response from any of the three contacts. The distance to the objects was unknown, which means all estimates of their size, altitude, and speed are inherently unreliable. There was no interaction between the pilot's aircraft and the objects.

The document does not offer any conclusion about what the objects were. It is a raw incident report, not an analysis. The reporter's name and email address are redacted under a personal-privacy exemption, but the narrative and most data fields are intact.
public_caveats: This is a single-source report based entirely on one pilot's visual observations at night — no crew member, ship, or sensor independently corroborated the sighting.
No radar track, electronic emissions, or transponder data was captured, so the objects were never instrumentally confirmed to exist.
The pilot did not know the distance to the objects, making any estimates of their size, speed, or altitude unreliable.
The pilot's identifying information is redacted, so the account cannot be independently verified by name.
The form itself notes that 'all descriptive and estimative language reflects the reporter's subjective interpretation at the time of the event.'
